docs.D00_original_thesis.md:
Title: Original position and the earliest recovered primary thesis updates
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2018/10/25020540/Pershing-Square-Announces-Position-in-Hilton-Worldwide-Holdings-Inc.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07150943/2018-Annual-Report-Letter-Only.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07155526/2019-Semiannual-Financials-Letter-to-Shareholders.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20192925/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-June-2025-Interim.pdf
Date: 2025-08-20

The October 25, 2018 announcement establishes a new investment of 10.9 million Hilton shares, 3.7% of the company. At then-current market value it represented approximately 13.9% of PSH NAV, with smaller weights in the private funds. The release does not itself give the detailed underwriting thesis; it promises discussion in the third-quarter letter and call. That original detailed document was not recovered. The quotations below are explicitly dated subsequent primary updates, not invented purchase-day language.

March 19, 2019 letter: “We took advantage of the year-end market downdraft by making a large new investment in Hilton Worldwide Holdings while other investors became forced or irrational sellers.” This attributes part of the opportunity to market conditions and patient capital. It does not say every share was bought at the year-end low.

The August 2019 H1 letter describes the core economics as an “assetlight, fee-based business model” able to compound EPS at a “mid-to-high teens’ growth rate for years to come.” The same update says a large development pipeline, substantial buybacks and a strong management team were underappreciated. Its valuation observation was 23 times consensus 2019 earnings, below its stated view of intrinsic value. That is a 2019 valuation, not a timeless hurdle.

By August 20, 2025, the H1 report continued to call Hilton an “incredible business that offers a unique combination of predictability, resiliency and capital light growth.” This is an ongoing favorable assessment of the business, not a commitment to own at any price.

The thesis can therefore be evaluated on distinct dimensions: owners fund most hotel investment; the brand/distribution system collects recurring fees; net room additions supplement RevPAR; modest corporate reinvestment leaves capital for repurchases; management executes without sacrificing brand economics. A comparison with current information should ask both whether these mechanisms remain intact and whether their expected growth is already capitalized in the share price. Historical thesis continuity alone does not answer the valuation question.
docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Hilton's fee model and hotel-owner economics
Source: compiled from: https://ir.hilton.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001585689-25-000158/q32025earningsrelease.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1585689/000158568925000008/hlt-20241231.htm; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20192925/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-June-2025-Interim.pdf
Date: 2025-10-22

Hilton primarily earns management and franchise fees from hotels operating under its brands, supported by loyalty, distribution, reservations and development capabilities. It also has ownership-related activity. Most hotel property investment sits with third-party owners rather than on Hilton's corporate balance sheet. A capital-light corporate model is not the same as a capital-light industry: owners still face construction, maintenance, labor, financing and occupancy risk.

The Q3 release reports 8,995 properties and 1,328,821 rooms at September 30. The pipeline was 515,400 rooms across 3,648 hotels. Hilton opened 199 hotels with more than 24,000 rooms during the quarter. System net room growth was 6.5% over the prior September. Pipeline rooms are prospective, subject to owner financing and completion; they are not current royalty-earning rooms.

The core economics have two growth sources. RevPAR combines rate and occupancy at existing comparable hotels; system growth adds rooms that can generate fees even if comparable-property growth is modest. Fees are therefore less directly exposed to the fixed costs of operating each building, though incentive management fees and franchise revenue still depend on owner performance.

Headline revenue includes reimbursements and other pass-through activity, so total-revenue operating margins do not cleanly express the economics of the fee franchise. Q3 consolidated revenue was $3.120 billion and adjusted EBITDA $976 million. Comparing that ratio with an asset owner's hotel margin would be misleading without separating reimbursements.

Christopher Nassetta remains president and CEO, with Kevin Jacobs CFO. There is no identified management-replacement thesis in the retrieved materials. PSH's August H1 commentary describes the leadership team and capital-light growth favorably. Governance quality and operating quality can therefore be considered independently of whether current valuation offers a sufficient prospective return.

Hilton reported 232.4 million common shares outstanding at October 17. This is a dated common-share observation, not a January 15 count. Repurchases can make per-share earnings grow faster than operating profit, but only if funded sustainably and executed at sensible prices. A smaller denominator is not itself evidence of higher intrinsic value if the repurchase valuation is excessive.

The main moat hypothesis combines brand demand, owner economics, loyalty/distribution scale and the development network. Weak hotel-owner returns, loss of brand relevance or slower conversions could impair that mechanism even while near-term reported EPS benefits from buybacks.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Three-year financial base and September-quarter comparison
Source: compiled from: https://ir.hilton.com/news-events/investor-news/detail/116/hilton-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-results; https://ir.hilton.com/news-events/investor-news/detail/104/hilton-reports-fourth-quarter-and-record-full-year-results; https://ir.hilton.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001585689-25-000158/q32025earningsrelease.htm
Date: 2025-10-22

Figures are millions of dollars except EPS. Annual observations come from February 7, 2024 and February 6, 2025 releases; the latest-quarter observation is October 22, 2025. Adjusted figures retain Hilton's definitions and should not be substituted indiscriminately for GAAP earnings.

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | Q3 2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 8,773 | 10,235 | 11,174 | 3,120 |
| Growth, calculated | — | 16.7% | 9.2% | — |
| Operating income | 2,094 | 2,225 | 2,370 | Not extracted |
| GAAP operating margin, calculated | 23.9% | 21.7% | 21.2% | Not available |
| Adjusted EBITDA | 2,599 | 3,089 | 3,429 | 976 |
| GAAP diluted EPS | 4.53 | 4.33 | 6.14 | 1.78 |
| Adjusted diluted EPS | 4.89 | 6.21 | 7.12 | 2.11 |
| Capex | 102 | 247 | 198 | 50 |
| Contract acquisition costs | 81 | 233 | 105 | 31 calculated |
| Net debt, period end | 7,534 | 8,392 | 9,860 | 10,600 |
| Net debt/adjusted EBITDA | 2.9x | 2.7x | 2.9x | — |

The quarter's $31 million contract-acquisition-cost figure is the difference between reported $81 million total capex/contract costs and $50 million capital expenditures. For nine months, revenue was $8.952 billion, adjusted EBITDA $2.779 billion, GAAP diluted EPS $4.84 and adjusted EPS $6.03. Nine-month capex was $133 million and combined capex/contract costs $236 million.

Shareholder returns remain a substantial use of cash. FY2023 repurchases were $2.3 billion and dividends $158 million. FY2024 capital return including dividends was $3.0 billion; dividends were $150 million and 13.3 million shares were repurchased. Quarterly dividends were $0.15 per share in the 2024 release.

Cash flow from operations and a consistent three-year FCF reconciliation were not extracted from these release tables. Neither adjusted EBITDA minus capex nor net income minus capex is labeled FCF here: cash interest, taxes, working capital and contract acquisition outlays matter. A properly measured FCF yield is consequently unavailable rather than silently approximated.

The balance-sheet trend is still informative. Net debt rose from $7.534 billion in 2022 to $10.600 billion in September 2025. Strong distributions and a capital-light fee model can coexist with rising debt. ROIC is not supplied under a consistent definition, and negative or buyback-reduced book equity would make a simplistic equity-return comparison especially misleading.
docs.D03_latest_results_and_guidance.md:
Title: Latest public results — modest RevPAR, strong unit growth
Source: compiled from: https://ir.hilton.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001585689-25-000158/q32025earningsrelease.htm; https://ir.hilton.com/~/media/Files/H/Hilton-Worldwide-IR-V3/quarterly-results/2025/3q-2024-earnings-call-october-22-2025.pdf
Date: 2025-10-22

The latest authenticated financial release before the January 15 cutoff is the September-quarter report issued October 22. Q3 net income was $421 million, GAAP diluted EPS $1.78 and adjusted EPS $2.11. Adjusted EBITDA was $976 million, up 8% according to the call and above the high end of guidance. These results demonstrate that modest existing-hotel demand need not translate directly into stagnant corporate earnings.

System-wide comparable currency-neutral RevPAR fell 1.1%. The call attributes pressure to calendar/event shifts, softer inbound international travel to the US, reduced government-related travel and renovations. US comparable RevPAR fell 2.3%; leisure transient RevPAR was roughly flat, while group RevPAR fell approximately 4%. These observations are evidence of demand softness, but not proof of a permanent loss of brand relevance.

| FY2025 outlook at October 22 | Guidance |
|---|---|
| System-wide comparable currency-neutral RevPAR | Flat to +1.0% |
| Net unit growth | 6.5–7.0% |
| Adjusted EBITDA | $3.685–3.715 billion |
| Net income | $1.604–1.625 billion |
| GAAP diluted EPS | $6.71–6.80 |
| Adjusted diluted EPS | $7.97–8.06 |
| Capex plus contract acquisition costs | $250–300 million |
| Capital return | Approximately $3.3 billion |

Management describes results as demonstrating resilience from net unit growth, cost discipline and the capital-light model. Its call says, “We expect to deliver 6.5% to 7% net unit growth for the full year.” Q4 RevPAR growth was expected to be approximately 1%. The combination is the relevant operating algorithm: additional fee-paying rooms plus modest comparable growth and capital return.

At September 30, the development pipeline reached 515,400 rooms, up 5% from a year earlier. Thirty-three thousand rooms were approved during Q3. The development backlog supports visibility but still depends on external owners' economics and construction execution.

The outlook represents management expectations as of October, not final fiscal-year results. FY2025 realized earnings, Q4 RevPAR and FY2026 guidance are not known in this snapshot. In evaluating prospective returns, an analyst can use the $7.97–8.06 adjusted EPS range as a public reference, but must not replace it with an unpublished full-year result or a later year of management guidance.
docs.D04_price_and_valuation.md:
Title: January 15 valuation at a much higher share-price base
Source: compiled from: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/HLT/history/?period1=1768176000&period2=1768608000; https://ir.hilton.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001585689-25-000158/q32025earningsrelease.htm; https://www.macrotrends.net/stocks/charts/HLT/hilton-worldwide-holdings/stock-price-history; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07155526/2019-Semiannual-Financials-Letter-to-Shareholders.pdf
Date: 2026-01-15

January 15's historical unadjusted close was $301.86. The stock opened at $302.75, traded between $300.48 and $306.28, and recorded 2,218,600 shares volume. January 14 closed at $300.13 on 1,527,600 shares. These historical rows, rather than a current quote widget or subsequently dividend-adjusted close, define the price observation.

Using October 17's 232.4 million common shares gives an explicitly calculated equity-value proxy of $70.153 billion. Adding September net debt of $10.600 billion gives an EV proxy of $80.753 billion. The dated share count, debt movement and intervening repurchases make these proxies rather than exact January market-cap/EV observations.

| Calculated multiple at $301.86 | Basis |
|---|---|
| 42.4x | FY2024 adjusted EPS $7.12 |
| 37.7x | Midpoint $8.015 of FY2025 adjusted EPS guidance |
| 44.7x | Midpoint $6.755 of FY2025 GAAP EPS guidance |
| 21.8x EV/adjusted EBITDA | EV proxy divided by FY2025 guidance midpoint $3.700bn |

The guidance-year calculations are not next-twelve-month analyst consensus. FY2025 has ended, but results are not yet reported. An exact January 15 forward consensus EPS series was not authenticated. The distinction matters when comparing to any other date or to peers.

Macrotrends' completed-year return table records approximately 36.11% share-price appreciation in 2024 and 16.49% in 2025 on its adjusted historical series. These percentages describe already completed years, not a prospective return. They imply roughly 58.6% cumulative appreciation, calculated by chaining the percentages. Absolute adjusted prices from a present-day series are not used as the cutoff quote.

For a dated own-history reference, the August 2019 PSH letter described Hilton at 23x consensus 2019 earnings and below its estimate of value. That is a single observation, not a verified five-to-ten-year range, and both growth expectations and market conditions can change.

An authenticated January 15 52-week high/low, full own-history multiple range, S&P 500 forward P/E, peer cutoff multiples and properly reconciled FCF yield are unavailable. No missing multiple is filled from a later presentation. The observable question is whether operating growth and repurchases can justify the materially higher earnings capitalization without relying on further expansion.
docs.D05_market_worries.md:
Title: Contemporary lodging concerns and the valuation burden
Source: compiled from: https://wncy.com/2025/10/22/hilton-cuts-2025-room-revenue-forecast-on-subdued-us-travel-demand; https://www.hoteldive.com/news/hilton-reports-third-quarter-earnings/803495/; https://ir.hilton.com/~/media/Files/H/Hilton-Worldwide-IR-V3/quarterly-results/2025/3q-2024-earnings-call-october-22-2025.pdf
Date: 2025-10-22

Reuters, syndicated by WNCY on October 22, reported that Hilton cut its full-year room-revenue forecast as weak US travel demand persisted. Its framing is that consumers are dialing back discretionary spending and tariff uncertainty threatens purchasing power. The report gives US RevPAR down 2.3% in Q3 and notes the US represents roughly 65% of rooms. This is a dated operating concern rather than an assumption that all travel regions are equally weak.

Hotel Dive's October 22 coverage describes “softer-than-expected” RevPAR during a “noisy” quarter and highlights the revised 0–1% full-year growth range. The company's February outlook had called for 2–3% RevPAR growth. Lower comparable-hotel growth can reduce confidence in the fee-growth and earnings outlook even when net unit additions remain strong.

The call identifies specific headwinds: unfavorable holidays/events, government-travel reductions, inbound travel softness and renovations. Some can reverse or normalize; others can persist with policy and macroeconomic changes. An investor should not classify every weak data point as either purely temporary or structurally permanent without examining the mechanism.

There is a distinction between a good business and a good prospective return. A fee franchise can compound despite flat RevPAR, but a high P/E can already capitalize that resilience and much of the unit-growth runway. The valuation concern is analytical: if EPS grows more slowly than expected or the multiple normalizes, shareholder returns may lag operating growth.

Owner economics introduce another risk. Hilton generally avoids the full investment burden of constructing hotels, yet its future system growth depends on other parties being willing and able to build or convert. High financing/construction costs or weak hotel cash flows can delay pipeline conversion without immediately damaging current corporate earnings.

Buybacks are not a complete answer to valuation. A large annual repurchase program supports EPS, but debt-funded repurchases at high multiples can reduce future flexibility. Net debt was $10.6 billion in September. Equally, a weak comparable-demand quarter is not proof of franchise impairment: Q3 EBITDA rose 8% and unit growth was 6.5%.

No authenticated January 15 independent sell-side quotation assigning a precise fair value is available here. The dated press provides demand concerns; the investment question adds the observable valuation burden rather than manufacturing an analyst downgrade or an undisclosed manager view.
docs.D06_peer_benchmarks.md:
Title: Marriott and Hyatt — modest industry RevPAR, differentiated room growth
Source: compiled from: https://news.marriott.com/news/2025/11/04/marriott-international-reports-third-quarter-2025-results; https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20251106873801/en/Hyatt-Reports-Third-Quarter-2025-Results; https://ir.hilton.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001585689-25-000158/q32025earningsrelease.htm
Date: 2025-11-06

Marriott and Hyatt are useful operating peers because their brand, management and franchise businesses also benefit from external owners' investment. However, geography, chain scale, owned-hotel mix, acquisitions and accounting definitions differ. Consolidated margins and enterprise multiples require adjustment before being treated as like-for-like measures.

| Q3 2025 | Hilton | Marriott | Hyatt |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Comparable system RevPAR change | (1.1%) | +0.5% | +0.3% |
| Adjusted EBITDA | $976m | $1,349m | $291m |
| Adjusted EPS | $2.11 | $2.47 | ($0.30) |
| Room-growth observation | 6.5% system net growth | Roughly 17,900 net rooms added in quarter | 12.1% including acquisitions; 7.0% excluding |

Marriott's November 4 release reports GAAP diluted EPS $2.67 and adjusted EPS $2.47. Adjusted EBITDA increased 10% and adjusted EPS 9%. Its call says global RevPAR's 0.5% growth reflected roughly 1% rate growth partly offset by lower occupancy. These observations suggest the modest-demand environment is not confined to Hilton, while Marriott's positive RevPAR contrasts with Hilton's negative quarter.

Hyatt's November 6 release reports $49 million GAAP net loss and $29 million adjusted net loss. Adjusted EBITDA rose 5.6%, or 10.1% after adjusting for assets sold in 2024. Gross fees were $283 million, up 5.9%. Its acquisition-inclusive room growth must not be labeled an organic rate.

The common industry mechanism is room additions plus fees on nominal lodging demand. Brand distribution, loyalty and owner profitability can create a reinforcing development loop. But owners can choose competing brands, conversions require investment, and larger pipelines do not automatically earn fees until hotels open.

Date-authenticated January 15 forward P/E, EV/EBITDA and reconciled FCF yield for these peers were not recovered. This table therefore benchmarks operations rather than claiming a complete relative valuation. It cannot establish that Hilton deserves its current premium merely because it has a high-quality fee model: competing franchisors also have capital-light attributes.

For an analyst evaluating an existing Hilton position, the useful questions are whether the RevPAR underperformance is mix/calendar-related, whether room growth remains superior after comparable definitions, and whether Hilton's expected per-share growth compensates for its earnings multiple. Strong industry structure helps business quality; it does not remove price discipline.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: Public developments through January 15
Source: compiled from: https://ir.hilton.com/news-events/investor-news/detail/104/hilton-reports-fourth-quarter-and-record-full-year-results; https://ir.hilton.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001585689-25-000158/q32025earningsrelease.htm; https://wncy.com/2025/10/22/hilton-cuts-2025-room-revenue-forecast-on-subdued-us-travel-demand; https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/HLT/history/?period1=1768176000&period2=1768608000; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20192925/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-June-2025-Interim.pdf
Date: 2026-01-15

February 6, 2025: Hilton reported record FY2024 results. Revenue was $11.174 billion, adjusted EBITDA $3.429 billion and adjusted EPS $7.12. It returned $3.0 billion including dividends and guided to 2–3% comparable currency-neutral RevPAR growth for 2025. That initial forecast supplies a public starting benchmark against which the subsequent reduction can be judged.

August 20: PSH's H1 report continued to describe Hilton's predictability, resilience and capital-light growth favorably. This is a public statement about business quality, not evidence of a fixed minimum holding period or an unconditional valuation endorsement.

October 2025: Hilton announced Outset Collection, a new lifestyle brand, as noted in the October 22 release. New brands can expand addressable owner demand, but brand proliferation is not automatically incremental profit; contracts, development economics and differentiation determine value.

October 22: Q3 results reported RevPAR down 1.1% system-wide and 2.3% in the US. Adjusted EBITDA nevertheless reached $976 million. Management narrowed full-year RevPAR expectations to flat through +1% and expected net unit growth of 6.5–7.0%. The contrast between weak comparables and stronger system growth is central to interpreting the business.

October 22 press: Reuters framed the guidance reduction as evidence of subdued US travel demand amid consumer and tariff concerns. The company call attributed additional pressure to government travel, calendars, renovations and softer inbound demand. These are contemporaneous explanations rather than resolved causal weights.

Year-end 2025: The completed-year historical price-return series shows continued appreciation after a strong 2024. A rising share price alongside a lower RevPAR outlook raises a valuation question but is not itself evidence of investor irrationality; expected unit growth, margins and per-share capital allocation also influence value.

January 15, 2026: Historical unadjusted close was $301.86 on 2.219 million shares. The December PSH fact sheet was publicly available on this date. Full-year Hilton realized results and new-year guidance are not included in this timeline because they are not yet authenticated public information at the cutoff.

No verified CEO turnover, announced activist demand or binding change in the franchise model appears in these retrieved developments. The decision is therefore a comparison of an established business and current valuation, with unknown future operating outcomes.
docs.D08_pershing_context.md:
Title: Existing ownership within a concentrated permanent-capital portfolio
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/15162701/PSH-Fact-Sheet-December-2025-Website.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20192925/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-June-2025-Interim.pdf; https://finance.yahoo.com/news/bill-ackman-bets-2-magnificent-212245570.html
Date: 2026-01-15

PSH's December fact sheet, released January 15, lists Hilton among publicly disclosed holdings. Other names include Alphabet, Amazon, Brookfield, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Hertz, Howard Hughes, Pershing Square SPARC, Restaurant Brands, Seaport, Uber and Universal Music. The list includes only publicly disclosed positions and is not a complete economic exposure report for that day.

The fact sheet reports $15.536 billion equity and $19.187 billion gross AUM, including debt principal. Its reported debt-to-total-capital ratio is 19.5%, and it lists thirteen issuer positions. These figures differ from manager-wide assets, current cash and US 13F value.

The most recent available US 13F at the cutoff is the September-quarter filing made November 14. Full line-item weights from that filing were not independently authenticated here. The older June-quarter secondary account reports about 21% Uber, 19% Brookfield, 11% Restaurant Brands and 9.3% Amazon in its reportable-book perimeter. These are stale contextual weights, not January PSH NAV weights. Exact current Hilton weight and current cash are unavailable in this snapshot.

H1 June net assets were $14.715 billion and cash/cash equivalents $1.404 billion. The H1 letter explains that permanent capital permits patient investment, but also discusses repositioning when market volatility presents better opportunities. It disclosed Canadian Pacific's April exit and maintained favorable Hilton business commentary. Later unpublished position information cannot be assumed from the passage of time.

The January fact sheet states the substantial majority of the portfolio is normally in 8–12 core holdings, usually liquid listed North American large caps. It seeks high-quality businesses with limited downside and predictable recurring cash flows, occasionally using managerial, operating or governance changes to create value. It also allows opportunistic hedging.

Hilton fits many of those qualitative preferences, but a portfolio decision must also compare prospective returns with other opportunities. Permanent capital removes redemption pressure; it does not eliminate the cost of owning a lower-return security. Neither a favorable business assessment nor a long ownership history is a stated instruction to ignore valuation.

No public pre-cutoff statement retrieved here commits Pershing to a minimum Hilton holding period, announces a new Hilton intervention or supplies a January intrinsic-value target. Those fields remain unknown rather than inferred from later disclosures.
docs.D09_what_has_changed.md:
Title: Re-underwriting an established franchise rather than replaying the original bargain
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/10/07155526/2019-Semiannual-Financials-Letter-to-Shareholders.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20192925/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-June-2025-Interim.pdf; https://ir.hilton.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001585689-25-000158/q32025earningsrelease.htm; https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/HLT/history/?period1=1768176000&period2=1768608000
Date: 2026-01-15

The earliest recovered detailed thesis update, in 2019, emphasized a fee-based model, development pipeline, buybacks and management supporting mid-to-high-teens EPS compounding. The cited valuation was 23x consensus 2019 earnings. The question today is not whether those exact 2019 conditions can be recalled, but whether the remaining growth and the current price still offer a suitable return.

What appears intact: Hilton is still a large brand/distribution franchise, development pipeline is substantial, most hotel investment is external, and management continues to emphasize capital-light growth. PSH's August 2025 letter still describes the business favorably. Q3's 8% adjusted EBITDA growth despite negative comparable RevPAR supplies concrete evidence that the model is more resilient than a simple hotel-owner operating-leverage story.

What is different: the financial base is much larger. FY2024 adjusted EPS was $7.12, while the October outlook for FY2025 was $7.97–8.06. At $301.86, the stock is 37.7x that guidance midpoint, a calculated guidance-year multiple. The 2019 observation and current calculation are not perfectly like-for-like forward horizons, but the difference is large enough to require explicit valuation work rather than an assumption that the old purchase discount persists.

Growth expectations also need updating. The initial 2025 RevPAR forecast was 2–3%; the October forecast was flat to +1%. Net room additions can offset some weakness, but the development pipeline cannot remove all exposure to demand, owner financing or macroeconomic conditions. A higher multiple increases the cost of forecast errors.

Capital allocation is another change in the evidence set. Annual distributions remain substantial while net debt rose from $7.534 billion in 2022 to $10.600 billion in September 2025. Repurchases support per-share growth but require evaluating their cost and funding, not merely their existence.

The counterargument is that long-duration room growth and fee economics merit a premium and that weaker RevPAR is temporary. The valuation counterargument is that even an intact excellent franchise can offer insufficient future return at the current price. No resolved answer is embedded here; the analyst must forecast earnings, choose a defensible terminal valuation and compare holding with alternative uses of capital.

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: 10 documents including D00 and changes-since-purchase. Retained January 15 because an after-results sale cannot be proven. No February release or exit language in agent documents. Original announcement retrieved; original detailed 2018 thesis not recovered, subsequent primary quotations explicitly dated. Three-year financials, Q3 release, price/liquidity verified. Missing reconciled CFO/FCF, cutoff 52-week range, consensus, full own-history multiples and peer valuation. S3 funding motive not independently substantiated for Hilton and not asserted.

thesis_at_purchase_vs_now: Fee-based model: intact, with demonstrated resilience in Q3 [D02], [D10]
Development pipeline: intact, with 515,400 rooms in backlog [D02], [D04]
Management execution: intact, with continued focus on capital-light growth [D02], [D10]
Valuation: changed; stock trades at 37.7x FY2025 EPS guidance, significantly higher than the 23x multiple in 2019 [D05], [D10]

drivers.driver: The current valuation at nearly 38x earnings significantly compresses prospective IRRs compared to our 20% hurdle for new capital.
Persistent RevPAR weakness and macro headwinds necessitate a more conservative outlook for long-term compounding.

final.memo:
We remain admirers of the Company as a dominant, fee-generative franchise [D02], [D10]. The business model has proven its resilience, generating 8% adjusted EBITDA growth in Q3 despite a 1.1% decline in system-wide comparable RevPAR [D04], [D10]. The capital-light nature of the brand-distribution loop and the robust development pipeline remain key pillars of our thesis [D02], [D10].

However, at a share price of $301.86, the stock trades at approximately 37.7x the midpoint of 2025 adjusted EPS guidance [D05]. This valuation is a material step-up from the 23x multiple at which we initially underwrote the investment [D05], [D10]. While the franchise is excellent, we cannot ignore that the market is now fully capitalizing a long runway of growth, leaving little room for error should macroeconomic headwinds—such as tariff uncertainty or continued soft travel demand—persist [D06], [D10].

Our investment mandate is to achieve high rates of return, and at these levels, the prospective IRR is unlikely to meet our 15-20% thresholds [D10]. We are choosing to trim our position to reallocate capital toward opportunities offering more attractive asymmetric profiles. We remain disciplined in our valuation; owning a great business at any price is not the Pershing Square way [D05], [D10].

final.memo:
Hilton remains an exceptional, capital-light, free-cash-flow-generative business with durable growth prospects and a high-quality management team [D02]. Our fundamental thesis regarding its resilient fee-based model and the power of its development pipeline remains intact, as evidenced by the company's ability to grow adjusted EBITDA by 8% in the third quarter despite a decline in comparable RevPAR [D04], [D10].

However, we must remain disciplined regarding valuation. At a share price of $301.86, the stock trades at approximately 37.7 times the midpoint of its 2025 adjusted EPS guidance [D05]. This valuation is a material departure from the 23 times earnings multiple at which we initially underwrote the position in 2019 [D05], [D10]. While the business quality is high, the current price leaves little margin for error, especially given recent RevPAR headwinds and the ongoing burden of elevated debt levels used to fund repurchases [D05], [D06].

As managers of permanent capital, our goal is to maximize long-term compounding. When the forward IRR of an existing holding dips below our required threshold of approximately 15% due to multiple expansion, we must evaluate whether those assets are better deployed elsewhere [D09], [D10]. Because we are nimble and have access to other opportunities in our portfolio that may offer superior asymmetric return profiles, we have decided to trim our position in Hilton to capture gains and reallocate capital [D09].
uncited_claims: We have a fiduciary duty to our shareholders to recycle capital from fully valued compounders into assets with higher expected rates of return.
